A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Agent S3 and the same behavior-narrative trajectory-selection framework. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable. The bBoN-to-BJudge renaming and relocated appendix material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original Agent S3 and bBoN results on OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena, and AndroidWorld, alongside ensemble experiments, failure analysis, and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds resource-budget experiments, updated ensembles, and experiments varying narrative-generation and evaluation models.

M1.justification: Behavior Best-of-N is renamed Behavior Judge, but transition-based narrative generation, visual augmentations, MCQ trajectory selection, and Agent S3's coding agent and flat policy remain unchanged. The appendix system prompts also retain their substantive content. New foundation-model configurations instantiate the existing procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 361-task OSWorld subset, 154-task WindowsAgentArena benchmark, and 116-task AndroidWorld benchmark. Added model and resource-budget experiments do not introduce different tasks, populations, or input environments.

E2.justification: v2 adds a trajectory-summary comparator, using 3-6 sentences, to the representation ablation alongside the retained screenshot-only and naive-captioning baselines. WebJudge, already evaluated in v1's selection analysis, also appears in v2's main comparison table.

E3.justification: v2 adds worker-versus-step-budget evaluations and Qwen3/GPT-5 combinations for narrative generation and judging. Its four-rollout ensemble study replaces Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude 4 Sonnet with Gemini 3 and Opus 4.5. A new ten-rollout GPT-5/Opus ensemble and a GPT-5 configuration of GTA1 further expand evaluated settings.

E4.justification: New analyses examine resource allocation across workers, alternative models for the two judging modules, and trajectory summaries as a representation control. The earlier standalone rollout-count plot is replaced by the budget analysis, while the WebJudge scaling comparison remains. Existing failure cases, MCQ-versus-pairwise tests, and citation ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Agent S3's 62.6% result as averaged over ten runs, information absent from v1's corresponding table, and specifies ten Qwen3 runs. This adds run-count disclosure without establishing an increase in repetitions. Neither version provides confidence intervals or significance tests for the headline comparison.

E6.justification: v2 reports 72.6% for the new GPT-5/Opus ensemble, 55.0% for trajectory summaries, and new Qwen3-rollout results ranging from 33.3% unselected to 51.5% with GPT-5 generation and judging. Ensemble results are replaced under changed model configurations. GPT-5-only 69.9% and Windows/Android results remain unchanged; detailed 50-step Table 1 comparisons are removed.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, trajectory and narrative definitions, coding-agent formalization, and MCQ-versus-pairwise complexity analysis are retained. Renaming the judge and introducing empirical resource-budget accounting do not add substantive mathematical results or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claim changes from approaching human performance at 69.9% to surpassing it at 72.6% versus 72.36%, throughout the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The claimed lead over prior work changes from 10 to 9.2 percentage points. Agent S3 alone is described as strong rather than state of the art.

C2.justification: v2 adds a budget-dependent qualification: a single agent can perform best when splitting resources leaves workers insufficient steps. It also interprets cheaper rollouts with stronger judging as an efficiency opportunity. Existing hallucination, code-GUI handoff, and shared-state limitations remain substantively intact.

D1.justification: New Appendix B documents the GPT-5 model snapshot, AWS host configuration and parallelism, 100 postprocessing workers, per-module costs and timings, and a 17-hour-33-minute total execution time. These substantially expand operational reproducibility information; existing interface details and system prompts are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Jain et al.'s Multi-turn Code Generation through Single-step Rewards to the test-time-scaling discussion and emphasizes trajectory evaluation as the bottleneck distinguishing its approach from within-rollout scaling. Most cited works and the original novelty positioning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and bBoN is renamed BJudge throughout. The abstract, parts of the introduction, and limitations are rewritten, and experimental questions are reordered. The main section hierarchy, method exposition, and existing appendix prose remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column to a two-column layout, with extensive figure and table repositioning. Table 1 is restructured, the workflow diagram is redrawn, and resource-budget and cost displays are introduced. Existing appendix tables and case studies are retained under revised placement and numbering.

improvement.justification: The resource-budget experiments, additional representation control, model-role ablations, and pipeline cost disclosures improve practical assessment and reproducibility beyond v1's primarily success-focused evaluation. These gains are tempered by removal of detailed 50-step comparisons and a stronger human-surpassing headline based on 72.6% versus 72.36% without uncertainty estimates. The improvement comes from better supporting analysis and documentation, rather than the higher ensemble score alone.
